title: The wireframe's palette: each part's lines from its own material and name; the cost measured as none; the Ridgeback's tier decided on frozen frames too
context: Owner, 2026-10-26, on ?wire=1 with two CAD references (a tank with dim blue body lines, white lights, yellow labels; a sentry in grey with cyan accents): "what does it cost in rendering/fps to render as Wireframes instead the default" and "currently all elements of the wireframe in-game are rendered in the same white, is it possible to have various elements with slightly different colors as in these references? I personally like the look and feel". A survey of the three models' solid materials (state().wireSurvey): the hull has twelve material groups (greys and teals, the nine shell lenses 35eaff emissive x2, the plasma emitters' 7cf9ff x4, an orange light, a yellow and a white part), the Rotor six (greys, a copper e0a367, the lens eaf2ff x1.5), the Ridgeback ONE white material over 38 named parts (HULL_ARMOR, SHIN_ARMOR_*, TRIPOD_CLAW_*, UPPER_ARM_*, HYDRAULIC_ROD/BARREL_*, MINIGUN_*, LASER_CANNON, MISSILE_POD_*, RECON_SENSOR, SERVICE_DETAILS).
outcome: src/fx/model-fixture.js wireLook(mesh, tint): a lit part (an emissive of lightness over 0.3 at intensity >= 1, or a name matching SENSOR|LENS|OPTIC|MUZZLE|LASER|MINIGUN|MISSILE|LIGHT|LAMP|EMITTER|BEACON|RADAR|ANTENNA) is an accent, its emissive (or the wire cyan) toward white, opaque; ARMOR/PLATE/SHIELD the dimmest blue-grey; HYDRAULIC/PISTON/ROD copper; CLAW/ARM/LEG/SHIN/THIGH/KNEE/HIP/FOOT/TRIPOD steel; everything else keeps its solid's hue nudged toward the cyan at a lightness of 0.22-0.52 so the bloom leaves the body lines alone. setWireframe(root, on, { tint }) builds one wire material per mesh and caches it by tint; the briefings and the Units survey keep their one cyan (tint off). ?wire=1 is tinted, ?wire=flat the one cyan (state().wire.mode). The cost, measured headless on one scene twice (the finished base, four Rotors, the four landed, a ground camera by the hull): solid 26.8 ms a frame / gpu 31.4 ms, wire 26.0 / 30.4, the same draw calls (892 / 860) and triangles (2.80 M / 2.78 M): no cost; a wireframe is the same triangles drawn as GL lines with an unlit material, the same vertex work and draw calls and fewer pixels shaded. The far-view pair (42.4 vs 31.9 ms) was not the same scene (3,611 vs 3,315 calls) and is not a reading. Found on the way: the Ridgeback's far tier was decided only in stepMech (dt > 0), so a frozen frame (a camera cut, a pause) with the eye brought near showed the static lod2 until the game ran again; mech-squad's tierOf(mc, m) now runs on frozen frames too (the shot of the four at 15-24 m showed far: true before, false after). Harness: state().wireSurvey { hull, tower, mech, mechColours }.
alternatives: One colour per model (hull, sentry, mech): the references colour PARTS, and the hull's lenses, the Rotor's copper and the Ridgeback's hydraulics are what read as a drawing.

Edge geometry (EdgesGeometry at a crease angle) instead of the triangle wireframe: cleaner lines, a new geometry per mesh and the skinned/animated parts would need rebuilding every frame; the triangle wireframe costs nothing and keeps the gait.
Reading the mech's palette from the GLB (one material): nothing to read; the part names are the only variety it carries.
evidence: npm test 308, npm run check (td-tab 5,345 under 5,450; a 736-char survey line reflowed to pass the long-line budget), npm run architecture green.
Scratch probe --wire-cost (untracked, removed): solid near {ms 26.84, gpu 31.41, calls 892, tris 2800k}, wire near {ms 26.0, gpu 30.43, calls 860, tris 2783k}; far samples not the same scene.

Scratch probe --wire-shots: the instanced parts' colours HULL_ARMOR 80979a, HYDRAULIC_* cdac84, TRIPOD_CLAW/UPPER_ARM 9eaeb5, MINIGUN/LASER/MISSILE/RECON_SENSOR d5eef1; the mechs at the shot far:true at eyeM 15-24 before the tier fix, far:false after; artifacts/browser/wire-1-sentry.png, wire-1-mech.png sent to the owner.
The tracked --wire step was green before the palette (counts only); not re-run on the final tree.
